# Amazon Aurora: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=aurora-q017 -->
### Question 1

A company's order application has users around the world, mostly in North America and Europe. The application runs SQL queries with joins on an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster in us-east-1. European users report slow page loads, and most of their requests are reads. European users also make a few writes, such as profile changes, and every write must reach the same database. Which solution gives European users low-latency reads with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a separate Aurora MySQL DB cluster in a European Region, and keep the two clusters in step with a custom synchronization job.
- Create an Aurora global database with a secondary cluster in a European Region, and read from it with write forwarding turned on.
- Move the order data to Amazon DynamoDB global tables with a replica table in a European Region, so that each Region reads and writes locally.
- Create an Aurora global database with a secondary cluster in a European Region, and make that cluster a second writer for the European writes.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Aurora global database with a secondary cluster in a European Region, and read from it with write forwarding turned on.

**Deciding phrases.** "most of their requests are reads", "every write must reach the same database", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for low-latency reads for European users with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: Aurora MySQL in us-east-1, SQL queries with joins, mostly reads from Europe, a few European writes, and every write must reach the same database.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict an Aurora global database with a secondary cluster in Europe, because it keeps a copy of the data in another Region for local reads.
4. I remove the second writer, because only the primary cluster of a global database performs writes. I remove DynamoDB global tables, because the joins would force a rewrite of the application.
5. Between the global database with write forwarding and a separate cluster with a sync job, the difference is who runs the replication; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, so I choose the global database, which forwards the few writes to the primary.
6. Check: European reads stay in Europe, every write reaches the primary cluster, and the team runs no custom code. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The reads need a copy of the data in Europe, and the writes need one writer. An Aurora global database gives [low-latency read operations for applications](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cmp-global-db-low-latency-reads-worldwide) far from the primary Region. For [occasional DML statements](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-db-occasional-writes-use-secondary-reader-with-write-forwarding), the application connects to a secondary cluster that [has write forwarding enabled](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-db-occasional-writes-use-secondary-reader-with-write-forwarding).

**Why not.**

- "Create a separate Aurora MySQL DB cluster in ...": It can work, but the team builds and runs its own replication between two databases, which a global database provides as a managed feature.
- "Move the order data to Amazon DynamoDB global ...": Removing joins is [at the heart of NoSQL data modeling](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-no-joins-heart-of-nosql-modeling), so the SQL queries with joins force a rewrite of the application.
- "Create an Aurora global database with a secondary ...": In a global database, [only the primary cluster performs write operations](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-db-only-primary-writes), so the European cluster cannot become a second writer.

**Twin.** If the stem said "European users read but never write" instead: a global database without write forwarding, because a secondary Region is [made up entirely of Aurora Replicas](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-db-secondary-region-readers-only).

**Takeaway.** Distant readers and few writes: an Aurora global database with write forwarding.

**Review.** [Aurora Global Database copies the cluster volume to read-only Regions](2-deep.md#aurora-global-database-copies-the-cluster-volume-to-read-only-regions-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with one DB instance in us-east-1. The database must be highly available, with automatic failover if an Availability Zone fails. The company must also be able to recover the database in us-west-2, with a recovery point objective (RPO) measured in seconds, if us-east-1 becomes unavailable. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Depend on the cluster volume, which keeps six copies across three Availability Zones, to restart the writer in another zone within seconds.
- Create a reader DB instance in another Availability Zone of us-east-1, so that the cluster has an Aurora Replica to promote.
- Add a cross-Region Aurora Replica in us-west-2 to the cluster, and promote that replica if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.
- Run a scheduled script that copies a cluster snapshot to us-west-2 every 15 minutes, and restore the newest copy after a failure.
- Make the cluster the primary cluster of an Aurora global database, and add a secondary cluster in us-west-2.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a reader DB instance in another Availability Zone of us-east-1, so that the cluster has an Aurora Replica to promote.
- Make the cluster the primary cluster of an Aurora global database, and add a secondary cluster in us-west-2.

**Deciding phrases.** "with one DB instance", "automatic failover if an Availability Zone fails", "recovery point objective (RPO) measured in seconds", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for two steps that together give automatic failover across Availability Zones and recovery in us-west-2, with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: Aurora PostgreSQL, one DB instance, automatic failover if a zone fails, and recovery in us-west-2 with an RPO in seconds.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict that the storage already keeps six copies across three Availability Zones, so only the Region needs work.
4. I remove the cross-Region Aurora Replica, because Aurora PostgreSQL does not support cross-Region Aurora Replicas. I remove the snapshot script, because the team runs it and its recovery point is minutes old.
5. Between the cluster volume and the reader in another zone the difference is the compute. My first idea breaks because the storage survives, but with one DB instance Aurora must recreate the writer, which typically takes less than 10 minutes. A reader in another zone gives Aurora a replica to promote automatically.
6. Check: the reader in another Availability Zone and the global database secondary in us-west-2 meet every constraint, and no script runs. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The two needs have two different tools. Inside us-east-1, a reader in another Availability Zone gives Aurora a replica to promote. Across Regions, Global Database replicates with latency [typically under a second](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-replication-latency-under-1-second), so the RPO stays in seconds. Both are managed features, so the team runs no scripts.

- [Adding a new reader DB instance](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-convert-to-multi-az-by-adding-reader-other-az) in another zone makes the cluster Multi-AZ, and Aurora [automatically fails over to an Aurora Replica](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-auto-failover-to-replica).
- Aurora Global Database lets the database [span multiple AWS Regions](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-faq-global-db-definition), with an RPO [typically measured in seconds](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-rpo-typically-seconds-guide).

**Why not.**

- "Depend on the cluster volume, which keeps six ...": The copies protect the data; with one DB instance, Aurora recreates the writer, which typically takes [less than 10 minutes](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-failover-time-without-replica).
- "Add a cross-Region Aurora Replica in us-west-2 to ...": Aurora PostgreSQL [doesn't support cross-Region Aurora Replicas](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-postgres-no-cross-region-aurora-replicas), so this step cannot be done.
- "Run a scheduled script that copies a cluster ...": The team owns a script to [manually copy Aurora snapshots](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-no-cross-region-automated-backup-replication), and its recovery point is as old as the last copy, not seconds.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the database must recover only from the failure of an Availability Zone" instead: the reader in another Availability Zone alone, because Aurora [automatically fails over to an Aurora Replica](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-auto-failover-to-replica).

**Takeaway.** Zone failure: an Aurora Replica in another Availability Zone. Region failure: Aurora Global Database. One tool does not cover both.

**Review.** [When the writer fails Aurora promotes a replica behind the same endpoint](2-deep.md#when-the-writer-fails-aurora-promotes-a-replica-behind-the-same-endpoint-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company runs an order application on an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with one writer and two Aurora Replicas. The backup retention period is 7 days, and the team takes a manual snapshot every Sunday. On Thursday at 14:05, a faulty release deletes thousands of order rows. The company must get the data back as it was at 14:04, a point in time before the error. What should a solutions architect do?

- Run a point-in-time restore on the existing DB cluster to roll the production cluster back to 14:04 in place.
- Restore the manual snapshot from last Sunday to a new DB cluster, and point the order application at the new cluster endpoint.
- Restore the DB cluster to 14:04 as a new DB cluster, and copy the deleted rows back into the production cluster.
- Promote one of the Aurora Replicas to a standalone cluster, because the replica still holds the rows from before the deletion.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Restore the DB cluster to 14:04 as a new DB cluster, and copy the deleted rows back into the production cluster.

**Deciding phrases.** "as it was at 14:04", "deletes thousands of order rows"

**Why.** The company needs the data at one exact second. Aurora point-in-time recovery restores to [any second during your retention period](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-pitr-any-second-within-retention-period), and Thursday at 14:04 is inside the 7-day period. The restore works by [creating a new DB cluster](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-pitr-creates-new-cluster), so the team copies the deleted rows from the new cluster back into production.

**Why not.**

- "Run a point-in-time restore on the existing DB ...": When you restore, [a new DB cluster is created](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-restore-always-creates-new-cluster), so no restore rolls the running cluster back in place.
- "Restore the manual snapshot from last Sunday to ...": The Sunday snapshot misses every order that was written from Sunday to Thursday, so this restore loses days of changes.
- "Promote one of the Aurora Replicas to a ...": Aurora Replicas [connect to the same storage volume](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-adding-replicas-read-same-volume-offload) as the writer, so the replicas lost the rows at the same moment.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an Aurora MySQL cluster that was created with Backtrack turned on" instead: backtrack the cluster, because Backtrack [rewinds the DB cluster in minutes](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-backtrack-in-minutes-no-new-cluster).

**Takeaway.** A point-in-time restore reaches any second of the retention period, and it creates a new cluster.

**Review.** [Backups are continuous and every restore creates a new cluster](2-deep.md#backups-are-continuous-and-every-restore-creates-a-new-cluster-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster that was created several years ago. The cluster has one writer and one Aurora Replica. A security audit finds that the cluster is not encrypted at rest. The company must encrypt the database with an AWS KMS key that the company manages. A short maintenance window for the cutover is acceptable. What should a solutions architect do?

- Turn on the rds.force_ssl parameter in the DB cluster parameter group, and reboot the DB instances of the cluster.
- Take a snapshot of the cluster, restore the snapshot to a new DB cluster with the KMS key, and move the application.
- Modify the existing DB cluster to turn on encryption at rest with the KMS key, and apply the change during the maintenance window.
- Add a new Aurora Replica that is encrypted with the KMS key, and fail over to the new replica during the maintenance window.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Take a snapshot of the cluster, restore the snapshot to a new DB cluster with the KMS key, and move the application.

**Deciding phrases.** "created several years ago", "not encrypted at rest", "A short maintenance window for the cutover is acceptable"

**Why.** An existing cluster keeps its encryption state: you [can't convert an unencrypted DB cluster](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-encryption-cannot-convert-unencrypted-in-place) to an encrypted one. The path goes through a snapshot. The team restores the snapshot to a new cluster and must [specify a KMS key when you restore](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-restore-unencrypted-snapshot-specify-kms-key). The application then moves to the new cluster in the maintenance window.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on the rds.force_ssl parameter in the DB ...": The rds.force_ssl parameter is used to [require SSL/TLS connections](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-postgres-rds-force-ssl-parameter), which protects data in transit, not the data at rest.
- "Modify the existing DB cluster to turn on ...": You [can't convert an unencrypted DB cluster](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-encryption-cannot-convert-unencrypted-in-place) to an encrypted one, so no modify setting makes this change.
- "Add a new Aurora Replica that is encrypted ...": You [can't create an encrypted Aurora Replica](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-replica-encryption-must-match-cluster) for an unencrypted DB cluster, so this replica is never created.

**Twin.** If the stem said "encrypt the connections between the application and the database" instead: turn on rds.force_ssl, because the parameter is used to [require SSL/TLS connections](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-postgres-rds-force-ssl-parameter).

**Takeaway.** To encrypt an existing Aurora cluster, restore a snapshot to a new cluster with a KMS key.

**Review.** [Encryption at rest is set at creation and covers the whole cluster](2-deep.md#encryption-at-rest-is-set-at-creation-and-covers-the-whole-cluster-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with one writer and four Aurora Replicas: two large replicas and two small replicas. The team adds and removes replicas often. Each web request opens a new database connection. Read-only queries from the web application must be spread across all the replicas, including replicas that are added later. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Connect the read-only queries to the reader endpoint of the cluster, and keep the writes on the cluster endpoint.
- Create a custom endpoint that contains the two large replicas, and connect the read-only queries to the custom endpoint.
- Connect all queries of the application, writes included, to the reader endpoint, so that every replica shares the work.
- Store the instance endpoint of each replica in the application settings, and choose one endpoint in the code for each query.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Connect the read-only queries to the reader endpoint of the cluster, and keep the writes on the cluster endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "spread across all the replicas, including replicas that are added later", "Each web request opens a new database connection", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The read-only queries need to reach every replica, also replicas that join later. The reader endpoint gives [connection-balancing among all the Aurora Replicas](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-reader-endpoint-balances-replicas), and each web request opens a new connection, so the queries spread too. Applications that use the reader endpoint [support connections to new Aurora Replicas](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-auto-scaling-use-reader-endpoint), so nothing changes when the team adds a replica.

**Why not.**

- "Create a custom endpoint that contains the two ...": A custom endpoint holds [a set of DB instances that you choose](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-custom-endpoint-set-of-chosen-instances), so the two small replicas get no queries.
- "Connect all queries of the application, writes included, ...": The cluster endpoint is [the only one that can perform write operations](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cluster-endpoint-only-one-for-writes), so writes sent to the reader endpoint fail on the replicas.
- "Store the instance endpoint of each replica in ...": It works, but the team must [hardcode all the hostnames](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-endpoint-abstracts-connections-no-hardcode) and edit them each time a replica is added or removed.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Monthly analytics queries must run only on the two large replicas" instead: the custom endpoint, because it represents [a set of DB instances that you choose](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-custom-endpoint-set-of-chosen-instances).

**Takeaway.** Spread reads over all replicas: the reader endpoint. Send some reads to chosen replicas: a custom endpoint.

**Review.** [The reader endpoint spreads connections not single queries across replicas](2-deep.md#the-reader-endpoint-spreads-connections-not-single-queries-across-replicas-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company is moving a new order-processing application to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster. Both the reads and the writes of the application grow with the number of orders, and the database must keep up with the full load at all times. The load is unpredictable: it stays low for hours, and then sudden spikes raise it to many times the usual level within minutes. Which capacity option is the MOST cost-effective?

- Use Aurora Serverless v2 DB instances for the writer and the readers, with a capacity range from a low minimum to a high maximum.
- Use provisioned DB instances sized for the usual load, and buy Reserved Instances for those DB instances for a 3-year term.
- Use provisioned DB instances sized for the highest expected load, and pay On-Demand rates for those DB instances.
- Keep one provisioned writer DB instance, and use Aurora Auto Scaling to add Aurora Replicas that share the read and write load as it grows.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Use Aurora Serverless v2 DB instances for the writer and the readers, with a capacity range from a low minimum to a high maximum.

**Deciding phrases.** "The load is unpredictable", "sudden spikes", "the reads and the writes of the application grow", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The load is unpredictable and the writes spike too, so the writer needs more capacity at the peaks, as the readers do. With Aurora Serverless v2 you [specify the minimum and maximum capacity range](../facts/aurora-serverless.md#aurora-serverless-specify-min-max-capacity-range), and Aurora scales each serverless writer or reader inside it. The company does not hold peak capacity through the hours of low load.

**Why not.**

- "Use provisioned DB instances sized for the usual ...": It looks cheapest, but Reserved Instances are [appropriate for steady-state database workloads](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-pricing-reserved-instances-steady-state), and instances sized for the usual load fall behind during the spikes.
- "Use provisioned DB instances sized for the highest ...": It keeps up with the spikes, but it holds peak capacity through hours of low load, and AWS notes [higher costs if you overprovision](../facts/aurora-serverless.md#aurora-serverless-overprovision-raises-cost).
- "Keep one provisioned writer DB instance, and use ...": Aurora Auto Scaling adds readers and helps with the workload [only on the reader instances](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-autoscaling-writer-not-scaled), so the write spikes still land on one fixed writer.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The load is steady-state and predictable around the clock, and it will stay at this level for at least the next 3 years" instead: provisioned instances with Reserved Instances, which are [appropriate for steady-state database workloads](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-pricing-reserved-instances-steady-state).

**Takeaway.** Spiky load on reads and writes: Aurora Serverless v2. Steady load for years: provisioned instances with Reserved Instances.

**Review.** [Aurora Serverless v2 changes capacity with load inside a range you set](2-deep.md#aurora-serverless-v2-changes-capacity-with-load-inside-a-range-you-set-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance with three read replicas that serve its dashboards. During write peaks, the read replicas fall up to 40 seconds behind the primary DB instance, and the dashboards show stale data. The company needs a scalable read tier with replica lag in milliseconds, behind one read endpoint, without rewriting its SQL queries. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Stay on RDS for PostgreSQL and add two larger read replicas, because Aurora Replicas would also copy every change into their own storage.
- Convert the primary DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and send the dashboard queries to the standby DB instance in the second Availability Zone.
- Migrate the database to an Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with Aurora Replicas, and send the dashboard queries to the reader endpoint of the cluster.
- Keep the read replicas, and add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster in front of the dashboard reads, with application code that fills and expires the cache.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Migrate the database to an Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with Aurora Replicas, and send the dashboard queries to the reader endpoint of the cluster.

**Deciding phrases.** "replica lag in milliseconds", "behind one read endpoint", "without rewriting its SQL queries", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Aurora Replicas read the cluster volume of the writer instead of keeping their own copy, which keeps the lag low. The dashboards [connect to the reader endpoint](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-reader-endpoint-balances-replicas), one name for all the replicas. The [code, tools, and applications](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-existing-mysql-postgres-code-works) that work with PostgreSQL work with Aurora, so the SQL stays as it is.

**Why not.**

- "Stay on RDS for PostgreSQL and add two ...": RDS takes each update and [copies them asynchronously to the read replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only), so larger replicas still lag at write peaks, while Aurora Replicas read the volume of the writer.
- "Convert the primary DB instance to a Multi-AZ ...": The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the dashboards cannot send their queries to it.
- "Keep the read replicas, and add an Amazon ...": ElastiCache adds a [caching layer to improve read performance](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), but it is a second store with code to run, and cached results can be older than the replicas.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the dashboards can show data that is several minutes old" instead: the existing RDS read replicas are enough, because they give [read-only access to the replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only) for the dashboards.

**Takeaway.** Replica lag in milliseconds behind one read endpoint: Aurora Replicas on the shared cluster volume, through the reader endpoint.

**Review.** [Aurora Replicas read the shared volume so replica lag stays low](2-deep.md#aurora-replicas-read-the-shared-volume-so-replica-lag-stays-low-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs a production Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster with one DB instance. The cluster volume keeps copies of the data across multiple Availability Zones. The database must recover automatically from a failure of the DB instance or of its Availability Zone, and service must return in less than a minute. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Make no change, because the copies of the cluster volume already let the DB instance fail over to another zone within seconds.
- Add an Aurora Replica in the same Availability Zone as the writer, and keep the application connected to the cluster endpoint.
- Create an Aurora global database with a secondary cluster in a second AWS Region, and fail over to that Region when the writer fails.
- Add an Aurora Replica in a different Availability Zone from the writer, and keep the application connected to the cluster endpoint.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add an Aurora Replica in a different Availability Zone from the writer, and keep the application connected to the cluster endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "with one DB instance", "recover automatically from a failure of the DB instance or of its Availability Zone", "less than a minute", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** You make the cluster Multi-AZ by [adding a new reader DB instance](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-convert-to-multi-az-by-adding-reader-other-az) in another Availability Zone. If the writer or its zone fails, Aurora promotes that replica. The cluster endpoint [connects to the current primary DB instance](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cluster-endpoint-connects-to-current-primary), so the application keeps its connection string.

**Why not.**

- "Make no change, because the copies of the ...": The copies protect the data, not the compute: with one DB instance, Aurora recreates the writer, which typically takes [less than 10 minutes](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-failover-time-without-replica).
- "Add an Aurora Replica in the same Availability ...": A replica in the same zone fails with the writer, and after a zone outage you must [manually create one or more new DB instances](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-single-az-cluster-create-instances-manually).
- "Create an Aurora global database with a secondary ...": A global database lets the database [span multiple AWS Regions](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-faq-global-db-definition), which adds a second Region to run for a failure inside one Region.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the database must also recover in a second AWS Region if the whole Region fails" instead: add a global database too, because it lets the database [span multiple AWS Regions](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-faq-global-db-definition).

**Takeaway.** Storage copies protect the data; an Aurora Replica in another Availability Zone protects the writer.

**Review.** [When the writer fails Aurora promotes a replica behind the same endpoint](2-deep.md#when-the-writer-fails-aurora-promotes-a-replica-behind-the-same-endpoint-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster in one AWS Region. The cluster has a writer and two Aurora Replicas in different Availability Zones. A new contract requires cross-Region disaster recovery: if the Region fails, the database must run in a second Region with a recovery point objective (RPO) of seconds and a recovery time objective (RTO) of minutes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a cross-Region Aurora Replica of the PostgreSQL cluster in the second Region, and promote that replica if the first Region fails.
- Add the cluster to an Aurora global database, with a secondary cluster in the second Region that can take over the primary role.
- Add two more Aurora Replicas in other Availability Zones, so that the cluster keeps running if the whole Region fails.
- Copy a cluster snapshot to the second Region every hour with a scheduled script, and restore the latest copy if the first Region fails.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add the cluster to an Aurora global database, with a secondary cluster in the second Region that can take over the primary role.

**Deciding phrases.** "cross-Region disaster recovery", "recovery point objective (RPO) of seconds", "Aurora PostgreSQL", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Global Database replicates to the secondary Region with latency [typically under a second](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-replication-latency-under-1-second), so few writes are at risk. If the Region fails, a managed failover promotes the secondary cluster, and AWS says this [method is recommended for disaster recovery](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-db-managed-failover-recommended-for-dr). AWS runs the replication, so the team owns no copy jobs.

**Why not.**

- "Create a cross-Region Aurora Replica of the PostgreSQL ...": Aurora PostgreSQL [doesn't support cross-Region Aurora Replicas](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-postgres-no-cross-region-aurora-replicas), so this replica cannot be created.
- "Add two more Aurora Replicas in other Availability ...": The cluster volume keeps its copies in a [single AWS Region](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cluster-volume-three-azs-one-region), so replicas in more zones of that Region are lost with it.
- "Copy a cluster snapshot to the second Region ...": The team owns a script to [manually copy Aurora snapshots](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-no-cross-region-automated-backup-replication), and its recovery point can be an hour old, not seconds.

**Twin.** If the stem said "if one Availability Zone fails" instead: the existing Aurora Replicas in other Availability Zones already meet it, because Aurora [automatically fails over to an Aurora Replica](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-auto-failover-to-replica).

**Takeaway.** Region failure with an RPO of seconds for Aurora PostgreSQL: Aurora Global Database, not a cross-Region replica.

**Review.** [Aurora Global Database copies the cluster volume to read-only Regions](2-deep.md#aurora-global-database-copies-the-cluster-volume-to-read-only-regions-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 10

A company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with one writer and four Aurora Replicas: two large replicas and two small replicas. The team adds and removes replicas often. Each web request opens a new database connection. Monthly analytics queries must run only on the two large replicas, which have the memory that these queries need. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Connect the read-only queries to the reader endpoint of the cluster, and keep the writes on the cluster endpoint.
- Create a custom endpoint that contains the two large replicas, and connect the read-only queries to the custom endpoint.
- Connect all queries of the application, writes included, to the reader endpoint, so that every replica shares the work.
- Store the instance endpoint of each replica in the application settings, and choose one endpoint in the code for each query.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a custom endpoint that contains the two large replicas, and connect the read-only queries to the custom endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "must run only on the two large replicas", "The team adds and removes replicas often", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The analytics queries need a chosen group of replicas. A custom endpoint represents [a set of DB instances that you choose](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-custom-endpoint-set-of-chosen-instances), and you can define one for [instances that use a particular AWS instance class](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-custom-endpoint-use-different-instance-classes-reporting). Aurora balances connections among the members, so the team names the endpoint once and changes no code when other replicas come and go.

**Why not.**

- "Connect the read-only queries to the reader endpoint ...": The reader endpoint [balances connections to available Aurora Replicas](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-reader-endpoint-balances-connections-not-queries), the small ones included, so analytics queries also land on the small replicas.
- "Connect all queries of the application, writes included, ...": The cluster endpoint is [the only one that can perform write operations](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cluster-endpoint-only-one-for-writes), so writes sent to the reader endpoint fail on the replicas.
- "Store the instance endpoint of each replica in ...": It works, but the team must [hardcode all the hostnames](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-endpoint-abstracts-connections-no-hardcode) and keep them current when replicas change.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Read-only queries from the web application must be spread across all the replicas" instead: the reader endpoint, because it gives [connection-balancing among all the Aurora Replicas](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-reader-endpoint-balances-replicas).

**Takeaway.** Reads on chosen instances, such as large ones for analytics: a custom endpoint.

**Review.** [The reader endpoint spreads connections not single queries across replicas](2-deep.md#the-reader-endpoint-spreads-connections-not-single-queries-across-replicas-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=aurora-q010 -->
### Question 11

A company is moving a new order-processing application to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster. Both the reads and the writes of the application grow with the number of orders, and the database must keep up with the full load at all times. The load is steady-state and predictable around the clock, and it will stay at this level for at least the next 3 years. Which capacity option is the MOST cost-effective?

- Use Aurora Serverless v2 DB instances for the writer and the readers, with a capacity range from a low minimum to a high maximum.
- Use provisioned DB instances sized for the usual load, and buy Reserved Instances for those DB instances for a 3-year term.
- Use provisioned DB instances sized for the highest expected load, and pay On-Demand rates for those DB instances.
- Keep one provisioned writer DB instance, and use Aurora Auto Scaling to add Aurora Replicas that share the read and write load as it grows.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Use provisioned DB instances sized for the usual load, and buy Reserved Instances for those DB instances for a 3-year term.

**Deciding phrases.** "The load is steady-state and predictable around the clock", "for at least the next 3 years", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** A load that stays steady for years fits a commitment. Provisioned clusters are [suitable for steady workloads](../facts/aurora-serverless.md#aurora-serverless-provisioned-suited-to-steady-workloads), so the company sizes the DB instances for the usual load. Reserved Instances for those DB instances then lower the cost of capacity that runs around the clock.

**Why not.**

- "Use Aurora Serverless v2 DB instances for the ...": Aurora Serverless v2 is meant for [variable or "spiky" workloads](../facts/aurora-serverless.md#aurora-serverless-choose-variable-spiky-workloads), and AWS calls provisioned clusters [suitable for steady workloads](../facts/aurora-serverless.md#aurora-serverless-provisioned-suited-to-steady-workloads).
- "Use provisioned DB instances sized for the highest ...": It works, but it pays On-Demand rates for years for a load that Reserved Instances suit, because they are [appropriate for steady-state database workloads](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-pricing-reserved-instances-steady-state).
- "Keep one provisioned writer DB instance, and use ...": Aurora Auto Scaling helps with the workload [only on the reader instances](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-autoscaling-writer-not-scaled), and this load does not grow, so there is nothing for it to add.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The load is unpredictable: it stays low for hours, and then sudden spikes raise it to many times the usual level within minutes" instead: Aurora Serverless v2, because it is meant for [variable or "spiky" workloads](../facts/aurora-serverless.md#aurora-serverless-choose-variable-spiky-workloads).

**Takeaway.** Steady load for years: provisioned DB instances with Reserved Instances. Spiky load on reads and writes: Aurora Serverless v2.

**Review.** [Aurora Serverless v2 changes capacity with load inside a range you set](2-deep.md#aurora-serverless-v2-changes-capacity-with-load-inside-a-range-you-set-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 12

A company runs a web application on a provisioned Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster with one writer and two Aurora Replicas. The application sends its reads to the reader endpoint. Read traffic rises sharply every weekday morning and falls at night. At the morning peak, the Aurora Replicas reach 90 percent CPU utilization, and the writer stays at 30 percent. Which solution will adjust the read capacity automatically with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on Aurora Auto Scaling for the writer DB instance, so that its DB instance class grows during the morning peak and shrinks at night.
- Create an AWS Lambda function that an Amazon EventBridge schedule runs to add Aurora Replicas every morning and to delete them every night.
- Create an Aurora global database with a secondary cluster in a second AWS Region, and send part of the read traffic to that cluster.
- Add an Aurora Auto Scaling policy that uses target tracking on the average CPU utilization of the Aurora Replicas in the cluster.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add an Aurora Auto Scaling policy that uses target tracking on the average CPU utilization of the Aurora Replicas in the cluster.

**Deciding phrases.** "the Aurora Replicas reach 90 percent CPU utilization", "the writer stays at 30 percent", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The replicas are busy and the writer is not, so the cluster needs more readers at the peak. Aurora Auto Scaling [dynamically adjusts the number of Aurora Replicas](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cmp-aurora-auto-scaling-adjusts-replicas) with a target tracking policy. The application already uses the reader endpoint, which lets it [support connections to new Aurora Replicas](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-auto-scaling-use-reader-endpoint) without a change.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on Aurora Auto Scaling for the writer ...": Aurora Auto Scaling helps with the workload [only on the reader instances](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-autoscaling-writer-not-scaled), and the writer is not the busy instance here.
- "Create an AWS Lambda function that an Amazon ...": It works on normal days, but the team writes and maintains code, and a fixed schedule misses peaks that come early or late.
- "Create an Aurora global database with a secondary ...": A global database lets one database [span multiple AWS Regions](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-faq-global-db-definition), a large change for a daily read peak in one Region.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the writer reaches 90 percent CPU from write statements" instead: a larger DB instance class for the writer, because Aurora Auto Scaling helps [only on the reader instances](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-autoscaling-writer-not-scaled).

**Takeaway.** Aurora Auto Scaling adds and removes Aurora Replicas for read load; it does not resize the writer.

**Review.** [Aurora Auto Scaling adds and removes Aurora Replicas for read load](2-deep.md#aurora-auto-scaling-adds-and-removes-aurora-replicas-for-read-load-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=aurora-q015 -->
### Question 13

A company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with the Aurora Standard storage configuration. The cluster has one writer and two Aurora Replicas, all provisioned, and it runs a steady-state load around the clock that will continue for years. The monthly bill shows that I/O charges are about 10 percent of the total Aurora spend. A team member proposes Aurora I/O-Optimized because it has no I/O charges. Which change is the MOST cost-effective?

- Switch the cluster to the Aurora I/O-Optimized configuration, because a cluster without I/O charges costs less than an Aurora Standard cluster.
- Replace the provisioned DB instances with Aurora Serverless v2 instances, so that the cluster no longer pays for its I/O operations.
- Keep the Aurora Standard configuration, and buy Reserved Instances for the writer and for the two Aurora Replicas of the cluster.
- Keep the Aurora Standard configuration, and move more of the reads to the Aurora Replicas so that fewer I/O operations are billed.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Keep the Aurora Standard configuration, and buy Reserved Instances for the writer and for the two Aurora Replicas of the cluster.

**Deciding phrases.** "about 10 percent of the total Aurora spend", "steady-state load around the clock that will continue for years", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Two facts decide. Aurora Standard is the best choice when I/O spending is [less than 25%](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-standard-best-when-io-under-25-percent) of the Aurora spend, and here it is 10 percent. The load is steady for years, and Reserved Instances are [appropriate for steady-state database workloads](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-pricing-reserved-instances-steady-state). They work [with both DB cluster configurations](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-reserved-instance-both-storage-configurations), so the discount does not depend on the storage choice.

**Why not.**

- "Switch the cluster to the Aurora I/O-Optimized configuration, ...": I/O-Optimized is the best choice at [25% or more](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-io-optimized-best-when-io-25-percent-or-more) of the Aurora spend, and the I/O share of this cluster is 10 percent.
- "Replace the provisioned DB instances with Aurora Serverless ...": Serverless instances use the cluster's [Aurora Standard or Aurora I/O-Optimized configuration](../facts/aurora-serverless.md#aurora-serverless-storage-io-follow-cluster-configuration), so the I/O charges stay.
- "Keep the Aurora Standard configuration, and move more ...": I/O operations are [counted the same way](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-io-counted-same-writer-reader) on a writer or a reader, so moving reads between instances does not lower the I/O bill.

**Twin.** If the stem said "I/O charges are about 60 percent of the total Aurora spend" instead: switch to I/O-Optimized, because it is the best choice at [25% or more](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-io-optimized-best-when-io-25-percent-or-more) of the spend.

**Takeaway.** Check the I/O share first: below a quarter of the spend, Aurora Standard costs less.

**Review.** [Aurora Standard charges for each IO and IO-Optimized includes it](2-deep.md#aurora-standard-charges-for-each-io-and-io-optimized-includes-it-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=aurora-q019 -->
### Question 14

A company runs an application on AWS Lambda functions that use an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with one writer and three Aurora Replicas. All functions connect to the cluster endpoint. During traffic peaks, thousands of short-lived invocations open new database connections, and the writer returns "too many connections" errors. Most of the queries are reads, and the three replicas are almost idle. Which combination of steps will solve these problems with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Put Amazon RDS Proxy between the Lambda functions and the DB cluster, and connect the functions to the endpoint of the proxy.
- Send every query of the Lambda functions, writes included, to the reader endpoint, so that the three replicas share all the work.
- Run a connection-pooling service on Amazon EC2 instances in front of the DB cluster, and point the Lambda functions at that service.
- Send the read-only queries of the Lambda functions to the reader endpoint of the DB cluster instead of the cluster endpoint.
- Change the writer to a larger DB instance class, so that the writer accepts more database connections during the traffic peaks.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Put Amazon RDS Proxy between the Lambda functions and the DB cluster, and connect the functions to the endpoint of the proxy.
- Send the read-only queries of the Lambda functions to the reader endpoint of the DB cluster instead of the cluster endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "thousands of short-lived invocations open new database connections", "the three replicas are almost idle", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Two problems need two fixes. Short-lived invocations can [exhaust database connection limits](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy), and RDS Proxy keeps a [smaller number of long-lived connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-candidate-too-many-connections) to the database. The read load sits on the writer, and the reader endpoint moves the reads to the idle replicas.

- RDS Proxy fits applications that [frequently open and close connections](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-frequent-connections-use-rds-proxy), and it lets them [pool and share database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-definition-pool-share).
- The reader endpoint [reduces the overhead on the primary instance](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-reader-endpoint-reduces-primary-overhead-scales-selects) by running the reads on the idle Aurora Replicas.

**Why not.**

- "Send every query of the Lambda functions, writes ...": The cluster endpoint is [the only one that can perform write operations](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-cluster-endpoint-only-one-for-writes), so writes sent to the reader endpoint fail.
- "Run a connection-pooling service on Amazon EC2 instances ...": It works, but the team runs and patches its own pooling servers; RDS Proxy is a [fully managed, highly available database proxy](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-faq-what).
- "Change the writer to a larger DB instance ...": High Lambda concurrency can still [exhaust database connection limits](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy) on a larger instance, and the reads stay on the writer.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the functions open few connections, but reads keep the writer CPU high" instead: the reader endpoint alone, because RDS Proxy pools connections and the reads still run on the writer.

**Takeaway.** Connection storms: RDS Proxy. Reads that load the writer: the reader endpoint.

**Review.** [The reader endpoint spreads connections not single queries across replicas](2-deep.md#the-reader-endpoint-spreads-connections-not-single-queries-across-replicas-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=aurora-q021 -->
### Question 15

A company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster. The writer is in Availability Zone 1. Two large Aurora Replicas of the same DB instance class run in Availability Zone 2 and Availability Zone 3, and one small Aurora Replica runs reports. If the writer fails, the large replica in Availability Zone 2 must become the new writer. If that replica is also unavailable, the large replica in Availability Zone 3 must be next, and the small replica must be the last choice. Which configuration will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Keep the same promotion tier on all three replicas, because Aurora promotes the largest replica first and the small replica is the smallest one.
- Keep the current promotion tiers, and run an AWS Lambda function on each failover event that fails over again to the large replica in Availability Zone 2.
- Set promotion tier 0 on the large replica in Availability Zone 2, tier 1 on the other large replica, and tier 15 on the small replica.
- Set promotion tier 0 on both large replicas, and give the small replica a tier that removes it from failover so that it cannot become the writer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Set promotion tier 0 on the large replica in Availability Zone 2, tier 1 on the other large replica, and tier 15 on the small replica.

**Deciding phrases.** "Two large Aurora Replicas of the same DB instance class", "the large replica in Availability Zone 2 must become the new writer", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The stem gives a strict order for three replicas. Each instance gets a [promotion priority tier](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-faq-promotion-highest-priority-first), and on a failure Amazon RDS [promotes the Aurora Replica with the highest priority](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-promotion-priority-highest-promoted-first). Three different tiers make the order explicit, so the two large replicas no longer tie.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the same promotion tier on all three ...": With equal tiers RDS [promotes the largest one](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-faq-promotion-tie-largest-wins), but the two large replicas are the same size, so RDS picks [an arbitrary replica](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-promotion-tie-break-arbitrary) of the two.
- "Keep the current promotion tiers, and run an ...": It can work, but a second failover adds another interruption and code to maintain, and promotion tiers give the same order without code.
- "Set promotion tier 0 on both large replicas, ...": If the higher tiers are unhealthy, Amazon RDS [will promote the lower priority replica](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-faq-low-priority-replica-still-promoted-if-needed), and the two large replicas still share one tier.

**Twin.** If the stem said "either large replica can become the writer first" instead: one tier for both large replicas, because among equal tiers RDS [promotes the largest one](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-faq-promotion-tie-largest-wins).

**Takeaway.** Set the failover order with promotion tiers: the lowest tier number is promoted first.

**Review.** [When the writer fails Aurora promotes a replica behind the same endpoint](2-deep.md#when-the-writer-fails-aurora-promotes-a-replica-behind-the-same-endpoint-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=aurora-q012 -->
### Question 16

A company runs an Amazon Aurora global database for Aurora PostgreSQL. The primary cluster is in us-east-1, and one secondary cluster is in us-west-2. The applications connect to the database through the global writer endpoint, and the company does not want to change their connection settings. An outage makes the primary cluster in us-east-1 unavailable, and the company must restore write access in us-west-2 as soon as possible. The company accepts the loss of recent writes that were not yet replicated. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Run a managed failover of the global database to the secondary cluster in us-west-2, and keep the applications on the global writer endpoint.
- Run a switchover of the global database to the secondary cluster in us-west-2, and keep the applications on the global writer endpoint.
- Remove the secondary cluster in us-west-2 from the global database, and change the applications to use the cluster endpoint of that cluster.
- Restore the most recent cluster snapshot to a new cluster in us-west-2, and change the applications to use the endpoint of the new cluster.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run a managed failover of the global database to the secondary cluster in us-west-2, and keep the applications on the global writer endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "An outage makes the primary cluster in us-east-1 unavailable", "restore write access in us-west-2 as soon as possible", "does not want to change their connection settings", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The primary Region has an outage, so this is an unplanned event. AWS says that the managed failover [method is recommended for disaster recovery](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-db-managed-failover-recommended-for-dr). It promotes the secondary cluster in us-west-2, and the global writer endpoint follows the new primary cluster, so the applications change nothing.

**Why not.**

- "Run a switchover of the global database to ...": Switchovers are meant for a global database whose clusters are all [in a healthy state](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-db-switchover-healthy-only-unplanned-use-failover), and the primary cluster here is down.
- "Remove the secondary cluster in us-west-2 from the ...": Removing the cluster [immediately stops the replication](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-db-detach-secondary-standalone-readwrite) and gives a writable cluster, but the team changes every application and rebuilds the global database later.
- "Restore the most recent cluster snapshot to a ...": Snapshots reach another Region when you [manually copy Aurora snapshots](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-no-cross-region-automated-backup-replication), and a restored cluster misses every write after its snapshot and takes longer to start.

**Twin.** If the stem said "For a planned maintenance event, the company must move the primary role to us-west-2 while both Regions are healthy, with no data loss" instead: the switchover, because its [RPO is 0 (no data loss)](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-global-switchover-rpo-zero).

**Takeaway.** Region outage in an Aurora global database: managed failover. Planned move while both Regions are healthy: switchover.

**Review.** [A secondary Region takes over by failover after an outage by switchover when healthy](2-deep.md#a-secondary-region-takes-over-by-failover-after-an-outage-by-switchover-when-healthy-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=aurora-q018 -->
### Question 17

A company runs a 3 TB Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance for its order application. The company wants to migrate the database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL in the same AWS account and Region. The migration must have minimal downtime: the application can stop writing for only a few minutes during the cutover. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Stop the application, take a DB snapshot of the RDS DB instance, and restore the snapshot into a new Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster.
- Convert the schema with the AWS Schema Conversion Tool, and then move the data with AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) ongoing replication.
- Export the database with pg_dump during a maintenance window, and import the dump into a new Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with pg_restore.
- Create an Aurora read replica of the RDS DB instance, and promote the replica to a standalone cluster when the replica lag reaches zero.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Aurora read replica of the RDS DB instance, and promote the replica to a standalone cluster when the replica lag reaches zero.

**Deciding phrases.** "Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL", "in the same AWS account and Region", "minimal downtime", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** An Aurora read replica of an RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance works [within the same AWS Region and account](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-postgres-read-replica-migration-same-region-account), as here. The replica stays current while the application runs. When the lag is zero, [you can stop replication](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-postgres-migrate-replica-lag-zero-stop-replication) and use the cluster for reads and writes, so the writes stop for the cutover alone.

**Why not.**

- "Stop the application, take a DB snapshot of ...": A cluster restored [from an RDS for PostgreSQL DB snapshot](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-postgres-migrate-snapshot-from-rds) holds only the snapshot data, so the application stays stopped through the whole 3 TB snapshot and restore.
- "Convert the schema with the AWS Schema Conversion ...": AWS suggests the [AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT)](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-migrate-heterogeneous-consider-sct) for a source with a different engine; this source is already PostgreSQL, so conversion and replication tasks are extra work.
- "Export the database with pg_dump during a maintenance ...": A dump and restore copies the whole 3 TB while writes are stopped, which is a long outage, and the team runs and checks the tools by hand.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the source is an on-premises Oracle database" instead: AWS SCT with [AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS)](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-postgres-non-postgres-source-use-dms), because the source engine differs.

**Takeaway.** RDS for PostgreSQL to Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime: an Aurora read replica, promoted when the lag is zero.

**Review.** [Data moves into Aurora by snapshot by Aurora read replica or by AWS DMS](2-deep.md#data-moves-into-aurora-by-snapshot-by-aurora-read-replica-or-by-aws-dms-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=aurora-q020 -->
### Question 18

A company runs an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster that was created with Backtrack turned on and a target backtrack window of 24 hours. Twenty minutes ago, a faulty batch job changed many rows in several tables. The company must return the whole database to a specific time just before the job started, and the application can pause while the data is repaired. Which solution will return the data the FASTEST?

- Run a point-in-time restore to a new DB cluster at the time before the job, and then point the application at the new cluster.
- Run a point-in-time restore that rolls the existing DB cluster back to the time before the job, so that the cluster keeps its endpoint.
- Backtrack the DB cluster to a time just before the batch job started, and keep the application connected to the same cluster endpoint.
- Create a clone of the DB cluster, and point the application at the clone, because a clone keeps the data pages from before the job.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Backtrack the DB cluster to a time just before the batch job started, and keep the application connected to the same cluster endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "created with Backtrack turned on", "return the whole database to a specific time", "FASTEST"

**Why.** The cluster was created with Backtrack, and the job ran inside the 24-hour window. Backtrack rewinds the same cluster to a specific time, and it [doesn't require a new DB cluster](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-backtrack-in-minutes-no-new-cluster). A point-in-time restore gives the same data, but Aurora builds a new cluster first, which takes longer.

**Why not.**

- "Run a point-in-time restore to a new DB ...": It returns the data, but a point-in-time restore means [creating a new DB cluster](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-pitr-creates-new-cluster), which is slower than a backtrack that [doesn't require a new DB cluster](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-backtrack-in-minutes-no-new-cluster).
- "Run a point-in-time restore that rolls the existing ...": Restoring an Aurora DB cluster to a point in time means [creating a new DB cluster](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-pitr-creates-new-cluster), so a restore does not roll back the existing cluster.
- "Create a clone of the DB cluster, and ...": A clone [shares the same data pages as the original](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-clone-shares-data-pages-separate-volume) as they are now, so the clone holds the rows that the job already changed.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a DB cluster that was created without Backtrack" instead: a point-in-time restore to a new DB cluster, because backtracking needs a cluster [created with the Backtrack feature enabled](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-backtrack-only-if-enabled-at-creation).

**Takeaway.** Rewind an Aurora MySQL cluster in place, fast: Backtrack, if the cluster was created with Backtrack turned on.

**Review.** [Backups are continuous and every restore creates a new cluster](2-deep.md#backups-are-continuous-and-every-restore-creates-a-new-cluster-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
